lead: GMDSS, the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System, gets a distress alert ashore without anyone having to hear your voice, and brings safety information to you. On a yacht you meet it as the DSC radio, the EPIRB, the SART and NAVTEX, with AIS working alongside.

sections.title: The alert goes out by itself

blocks.p: Before GMDSS a distress call depended on somebody listening. Its main idea is **automatic alerting**: a DSC radio or an EPIRB sends who you are and where you are to a rescue centre, even if no one hears a voice call.

What reaches the shore depends on where you sail. **Sea area A1** is the water within range of VHF DSC coast stations, where most coastal cruising takes place. Further out, your VHF no longer reaches a coast station. A 406 MHz EPIRB, working through satellites, still alerts a rescue centre from anywhere.

fig.note: Sea area A1: in range of a VHF DSC coast station

head: Sea area
Defined by
rows: Range of VHF DSC coast stations
Range of MF DSC coast stations
Everything beyond, mainly the polar regions

blocks.p: An **EPIRB** is the yacht's emergency beacon. Switched on, it transmits on **406 MHz** a coded alert that the Cospas-Sarsat satellites pick up and pass to a rescue centre. A beacon with built-in GPS sends its own position in the alert, so rescuers get it faster and more precisely; without GPS the satellites have to work the position out.

fig.note: 406 MHz raises the alarm · 121.5 MHz guides the rescuers in

blocks.p: The beacon also sends a weak **121.5 MHz** signal, which a lifeboat or helicopter homes in on for the final approach.

A Category I EPIRB sits in a bracket with a hydrostatic release: if the yacht sinks, it floats free and switches itself on. A **PLB** alerts through the same satellites, but it is worn by a person and registered to that person; the EPIRB is registered to the boat.

sections.title: Register it, test it, own up to a false alert

head: Job
How
rows: Keep your details and the boat's up to date: rescuers use them to phone the owner and identify the yacht. A used boat's beacon must be re-registered to you
Only the built-in self-test, as the maker's manual says. Switching the beacon on sends a live alert
Switch it off and tell the coastguard or MRCC at once: the alert may already be in the system

sections.title: A line of dots on the radar

blocks.p: A **SART** goes with you into the liferaft. It answers a ship's 9 GHz (X-band) radar and paints a line of **12 dots** on her screen. The SART is at the dot nearest the ship; the line runs on beyond it. Its range depends on height, so mount it on its pole or hold it as high as you can.

fig.note: Radar screen · the line points away from the ship

blocks.p: An **AIS-SART** does the same job another way: it transmits AIS messages with its own position and shows on any AIS display nearby, with no radar needed.

**NAVTEX** is a receiver that prints or stores safety information. International broadcasts go out on **518 kHz**, in English. All stations share that frequency and transmit in turn, so you choose which station letters, and which message types, the set keeps. Select the local stations and it stops printing warnings for seas far away.

**AIS** sets broadcast a vessel's identity, position, course and speed on VHF, and plotters show them as targets. Ships carry **Class A**. Yachts usually fit **Class B**, a simpler small-craft set that transmits at lower power and reports less often.

fig.note: No targets on the plotter, yet a boat ahead

blocks.p: An empty AIS screen does not mean an empty sea. Many boats carry no AIS, and a set can be switched off. Keep a proper lookout whatever the plotter shows.
